title: Output of the `knowledge.search` MCP tool
description:
The whole response, not a fragment of it. A client validates what arrives, and publishing only the hit shape leaves the keys around it — `count`, `results`, and the `retrieval` block that says how the answer was produced — as an undeclared contract that drifts without anything noticing.

Both answer paths produce this shape: ranked retrieval against a published index, and the unranked canonical scan used when no index can answer. The fallback is not a degraded contract but the same one, because a project that has applied migrations and not yet indexed would otherwise answer every query with nothing — which an agent reads as "we have no such decision" rather than "ask me again in a moment".

Five required keys, always all five, and a sixth — `integrity` — that appears only when a bounded damage check fired (#30) and is absent, asserting nothing, otherwise.

projectId.description: Echoed from the request. Always a registered id: an unregistered one is an error, never an empty result (ADR-0002, SEC-13).

query.description: The string that was actually searched for, which is not always the string that was sent. It is truncated at 2,000 characters and re-encoded to replace anything that cannot cross UTF-8 — a lone surrogate, for instance — *before* the search runs, so the echo and the search agree. Without the cap, a 20 MB query came back verbatim as a 20 MB response to one search.

count.description:
The number of entries in `results`. Bounded by `limit`, which is clamped to 50 — a caller asking for 10,000 wants "everything", and refusing helps nobody while honouring it would blow their context budget.

Computed from the results the caller receives. It is never a count of what matched: a count that moves when withheld content matches is a truth oracle, and the trigram retriever matches any three-character substring.

Neither half of that is checkable by a validator, so neither is stated here as a constraint. That `count` equals the length of `results` could be spelled out, but only as fifty-one conditional branches saying what a client computes in one line; it is asserted against real responses in the wire-contract tests instead. That `count` is *independent of withheld content* is not expressible in any schema at all — it is a relation between two responses, and a validator sees one. What holds it is where the bound is applied: `limit` truncates results the canonical store has already admitted, never the candidates a retriever ranked. Truncating candidates is how this was last broken, and the schema said this sentence throughout. Read it as a claim the project owes a differential test, not as one this file enforces.

results.description: Best first on the ranked path; in canonical scan order on the unranked one. Every entry is resolved through the canonical store, so it reflects the revision as it is now rather than as the index recorded it (FR-R5).

integrity.description:
Present **only** when a bounded integrity check detected a discrepancy: the derived state database holds a different number of `migration_history` rows for this project — fewer, or more — than the active pointer that chose that database records in its `migrationCount` (#30). That comparison is the whole of what this key measures. The state database is immutable once built, so the two agree on a healthy project and any difference is damage: fewer when a row is lost or falls out of a `WHERE` (a corrupt `migration_history.project_id`), more when another project's rows reach this one — which is why it is a difference and not a shortfall. The check is a single covering-index `COUNT` over one project's migration rows (`O(migrations)`, off the retrieval hot path), so it reopens none of the timing channels the search paths close.

**It does not detect a result-emptying corruption of `knowledge_items`.** A sentinel in `knowledge_items.project_id` or `knowledge_items.item_id` drops the item out of every query while the migration rows stay intact, so this tool answers `count: 0, results: []` — a false "we have no such decision" — with *this key absent* and nothing in `retrieval` saying otherwise (`stale: false` on the ranked path, `null` on the unranked one, neither of which reports damage). Those positions are the `SILENTLY_EMPTIED` members carried to PR2 (#30), and nothing on this response distinguishes them from a project that genuinely holds nothing.

**Absence asserts nothing.** No `integrity` key means the check did not fire, which is *not* a clean bill of health and must not be read as one. The check is incomplete by design — this release (PR1) detects only a migration-count mismatch — so damage it does not yet cover leaves this key absent exactly as a healthy project does. There is deliberately no `damageDetected: false` form: a `false` token would read as "checked and clean" over an admittedly incomplete detector, louder than any description here, while absence, asserting nothing, cannot be misread without a caller inventing a claim. This is the same present-only contract `raptorPath` already follows on a hit (ADR-0008 decision 8): the wire already branches on key presence.

Declared so `additionalProperties: false` continues to hold when the key is present.

damageDetected.description: Always `true` when this key is present — the object exists to report detected damage, so the field is redundant with presence by design. Kept explicit rather than reduced to a bare boolean so the signal can grow a second field (a code, a bound) without a wire break, and never carries `false`: there is no clean form of this object, only its absence.

remedy.description: The single action that rebuilds the derived state from the Git-tracked migrations — the same cure a missing state database already names. The derived state is reconstructible (ADR-0004), so the remedy is always cheap and always the same, and it never quotes the damaged cell.
